newsitem.title: USA: FDA should stay off tobacco farms-lawmakers.
newsitem.headline: FDA should stay off tobacco farms-lawmakers.

text.p: Lawmakers from tobacco-growing states told tobacco farmers Friday they would try to keep the U.S. Food and Drug Administration off tobacco farms.

"It's time to tell the FDA to stop. No government agency should be telling you how to run your farm when you're making an honest living," said Rep. Mike McIntyre, a North Carolina Democrat. "Thomas Jefferson said that government which governs best governs least. FDA, do you hear the message?"

The politicians made the pledge at the 51st annual meeting of the Flue-Cured Tobacco Cooperative Stabilization Corporation. The group is a farmer-owned organization that administers the U.S. Department of Agriculture's flue-cured tobacco price support system.
Small metal ashtrays were placed on the seats of chairs throughout the Kerr Scott Building at the North Carolina State Fairgrounds, where the meeting was held.
The politicians, including four Democratic congressmen from Southeastern states and two state agriculture commissioners, decried moves to increase regulation of the industry.

On April 25, U.S. District Judge William Osteen in Greensboro, N.C., ruled that the FDA can regulate sales and labeling of cigarettes but cannot regulate promotion and advertising. The decision stunned the industry and was hailed by tobacco foes as landmark in the tobacco fight.

McIntyre, a member of the House Agriculture Committee, warned farmers that bills were being drafted to eliminate the tobacco support program. He said passage of the bills would be devastating, affecting 250,000 jobs which generate $7.7 billion in tobacco income.
Rep. Virgil Goode, a Democrat from Virginia, also blasted the FDA for its focus on tobacco.

"When is the FDA going to come out against beaches, saying that lying on beaches will give you melanoma? Or that eating hot dogs or eggs will cause heart attacks?" Goode said. "Smoking is a matter of personal choice."
Goode, also a member of the Agriculture Committee, told the farmers a bill for a 43-cent-per-pack increase in the cigarette tax was coming up in the House.

"There are bills in the Senate and House attacking crop insurance and agriculture extension," Goode said. "But driving tobacco farmers out of business is not going to stop people from smoking. Tobacco will just come from Mexico and China and other countries."
Rep. Bob Ethridge, a North Carolina Democrat and one of two tobacco farmers in the House, said fewer members of Congress than ever have any agriculture ties.
"A lot of the people in Congress don't understand the issues," said Ethridge, who added that in the current political climate he would consider a compromise deal to support the tobacco program.
"But if it doesn't protect allotments and the growers, it's dead on arrival as far as I'm concerned."
Florida Rep. Allen Boyd urged farmers to spread the word about the economic benefits of the tobacco industry by talking to politicians, civic groups and the media.
Despite two hurricanes and heavy rains, last year's flue-cured tobacco crop was among the best ever, the industry said.

Gross marketings totaled 973.4 million pounds which sold for a market average of $183.72 per hundred pounds, compared to 1995 figures of 924.8 million pounds for a market average of $179.40 per hundred pounds.
